utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: I didn't hear that. He didn't give any orders. Before he killed this Stipo, he did ask us to kill Stipo, but we didn't dare. But whether he gave orders to anyone else, I don't know. I don't know whether he ordered anybody to kill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [No interpretation provided]

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know how to put it. I think that he didn't force any one of his own to kill because he was the most powerful there. Even his own were afraid of him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I come back to my initial question: So he was the absolute master in that place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You also said that Jelisic claimed that he had killed a certain number of victims, I think it was you who said 76 or 86, but that wasn't the figure that he wanted to accomplish. However, he came with that Serbian officer to read the order to stop the killings. This order, did it come from him, do you think, or was it imposed upon him contrary to his own will?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) This Serb officer, was he a Serb, according to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. But anyway, he was wearing an officer's uniform. He probably was, but I don't know. I don't know his name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes. But he seemed to have some authority over Jelisic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: I can't tell you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You also said that Jelisic left shortly after this order, that he left the Luka camp; therefore, his mission was terminated, or was he sent away? What did it seem to you to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: When he read this order, he left the hangar -- of course, he was seen around town -- he would come back to the hangar but he wouldn't kill anyone. He would drop in because Kole was the director after that. But anyway, there were no more killings. He would come and go. He would walk around. He would come to Luka. But ever since the date the order was read, he didn't do any killing in Luka. I don't know what happened anywhere else because I didn't see it. But I was talking about Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) And my last question: You said there were between 400 and 500 detainees in the hangar and that about 100 were released. What happened to the remaining 300 or 400; do you have any idea whether they disappeared or whether they were found alive or what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those who remained alive were alive, but some people did go missing, of course. I don't know where they went to, but they disappeared. In any case, they didn't come back to the hangar. They left the hangar. They were taken away and they didn't come back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm talking about those who were released and others who were taken out, or was there a difference between them, or perhaps you don't know who was released and those who went missing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: Those who were released home went home and then they would take out groups of 20 or 30 men who were also released, but later on, those men were brought back into the hangar, some of them who had been released.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Judge Riad. Judge Rodrigues, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Mr. President. I have at least three questions. Witness, I shall follow on to the question put to you by my colleague, Judge Riad, to ask you how did you know that the people were released?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: I saw them being called out by name and given these discharge papers to go home. I begged God that I be among the lucky ones to be sent home. People came with these certificates allowing them to go home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) After your release from the camp, did you find the people who were released before, before you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: When I left the camp, I came across a person who was with me in the camp. I stayed with him in his home because I didn't dare stay in my own because there was a frontline in my street. So we stayed there for about 20 days, we stayed in these houses. The army came; two soldiers came. They took us out. It was morning. We entered a bus, and we were taken to Batkovici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) You used, as a reference number to calculate the number of detainees in the camp, a box into which you threw your personal documents; do you remember that? There was a box.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Could you roughly tell us the size of that box?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was maybe half a metre by a half a metre and it was about 30 centimetres deep and it was full as we threw our documents into it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I don't know whether I understood you well. You put your identity card to the side because the box was already full.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was full, the box was full.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Therefore, out of this number and among all these detainees, you said that the majority were Muslim but there were also a few Croats; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, correct, but the majority were Muslims, by far the greatest number were Muslim. There were few Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Were there any Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I can't say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) And when some detainees were released, were the Croats released or did they stay behind as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: They read out the names of people from their ID cards. I didn't remember whether there were any Croats, but I do believe that some did go, that a large number of them were released. But by far, most of the detainees were Muslims; there were very few Croats. The Muslims were the largest group.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) So you know when somebody is a Croat or not when you hear the name; is that so? Is it by the names that you knew whether a person was a Muslim or a Croat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, of course I would know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you. I have no further questions. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Judge Riad has another question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Witness, how can you distinguish between those who left to be free, to be released, and those who were taken out to be executed when you were asked to get out of the hangar? How could you tell the difference?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were people whose names were read out, and they were told that they would be given these papers, discharge papers, and they did receive those papers, and the people who were called out to come out of the hangar did not return. They never came back to the hangar, so I don't know where they went.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Neither of them came back to the hangar so how could you know who survived and who was killed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: On that day, the people whose names were called out did not come back. They left. They went home. After a few days, I saw some of them come back because they said that they had been released and then captured again in their homes and brought back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) But the number of those killed, you said 76 or 86, was that the number that Jelisic himself mentioned? It wasn't you who counted these victims. You said yourself that he declared that he had killed between 76 and 86 people, but that was not his ultimate target.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Did he invent this number?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS B (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I simply heard him say that. I don't know what the target figure he had in mind was. We just listened to what he was saying. We didn't dare say anything. We just had to watch and listen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Witness B. You have suffered a great many things. I won't have any questions for you. You have been asked many questions. The Judges hope that you will have a safe journey home, that you will be able to restore some tranquillity to your life. Thank you once again for coming to testify in this Tribunal, and rest assured that all protective measures have been taken so that you shouldn't have any consequences from the fact of having the courage to come here. Stay seated for awhile while the Judges leave for the courtroom, and we will now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The hearing is resumed. Can the accused be brought in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) As everybody has noticed, there is one Judge missing. I have to inform you all of the fact that Judge Riad has been taken ill very suddenly. It is, therefore, necessary for him to go to the hospital to have a number of check-ups. In this situation, of course, we cannot proceed with the hearing. In fact, I have been told by the Registry that the situation is, in fact, quite one that is agreeable to the Prosecution in the sense that they don't have to call in another new witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOWERS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Greaves?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I, on behalf of the Defence, express the wish that Judge Riad is going to be fit and well soon, and I hope that I can say that on behalf of myself and my colleagues from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm sure that everybody sympathises with Judge Riad's situation. We all greatly appreciate his intelligence and his kindness, and I will transmit our best wishes to Judge Riad. We will suspend the hearing, and I'm sure, Mr. Greaves, this will enable you to fully take note of all the particulars of this case, and I think we will meet again on January 25th, if I'm not mistaken. Mr. Registrar, could you help us with that?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, we will sit from the 25th to the 29th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Yes, we will meet again on January 25th at 2.00 in the afternoon. Mr. Greaves, anything you wish to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I thank you for your good wishes. I am catching up rapidly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm sure you will. I'm sure that Judge Riad will be happy to know that everybody is agreeing to work hard until we meet again. I am about to suspend the hearing. I would just like to add that my colleagues and myself have one wish we would like to express. When witnesses are brought in and when you put questions to the witnesses, we would like these questions to be focused on the issue of genocide. This is the key issue in this case. Genocide is what Mr. Jelisic is accused of. Therefore, in the examination-in-chief or in cross-examination, what interests us most is this particular issue, the elements which constitute the crime of genocide. You have a few weeks to think about this particular issue. I would just like to turn to the accused. Mr. Jelisic, could you please stand up? How do you feel, Mr. Jelisic, and how is life in the detention unit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the things in the detention unit are going very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: And if I may be allowed, on my own behalf, to say that I am sorry for the condition that befell Judge Riad and to wish him a speedy recovery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I thank you on his behalf. The hearing is suspended. We will meet again on January 25th at 2.00 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.34 p.m., to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of January, 1998 at 2.00 p.m.
